tagline.text: A river town for playing in valley waterfalls and soaking in a cast-iron cauldron

children.text: A small mountain village in Antique province in northwestern Panay, calling itself the "Eco-Adventure Capital of Panay." In a day or two you can trek the seven-tier Bugtong Bato Falls, kayak and tube the Tibiao River, and soak in a kawa bath — herb-infused water heated in a large cast-iron cauldron.

Tibiao is a farming and fishing village of about 30,000 people on the coast of northern Antique, between Culasi and Barbaza. A short way inland from the coastal road, the mountain range running north-south through western Panay rises up abruptly, and the Tibiao River, flowing down from those mountains, carves rocky valleys and waterfalls on its way to the sea. The town has built on this terrain, branding itself the "Eco-Adventure Capital of Panay Island" and growing simple experience-based tourism centered on the river, waterfalls, and mountain rice fields.

The signature attraction drawing travelers is Bugtong Bato Falls in Barangay Tuno. A tiered waterfall with seven levels in all, travelers usually climb up to the lower three tiers and swim in the emerald pools. Coming down from the falls, a kawa bath awaits — soaking in herb-infused water heated over a wood fire in a large cast-iron cauldron called a kawa. Originally used for boiling down sugarcane juice into muscovado sugar, these cauldrons were repurposed as bathtubs, and sitting inside one while gazing at the rice fields and mountains has become a Tibiao specialty found nowhere else.

In the mountain barangay of General Fullon, about 600 hectares of rice terraces cultivated for generations by the indigenous Iraynon-Bukidnon community spread across the slopes, and far out at sea, Seco Island, a sandbar island about 1.5km long that belongs to Tibiao, floats offshore. Spending one day in the valley and river, and another in the mountain rice fields or on the island, gives you a well-rounded taste of northern Antique's nature.

This suits travelers who prefer active nature experiences over resort-style relaxation, those wanting a day or two away from Boracay in quiet countryside, and families looking to play in the water with kids. Public transport is inconvenient and amenities are limited, so it's best visited with a relaxed schedule.
From the registration office, cross the river and walk about
30 minutes
along rice paddy dikes and forest trails to reach the first tier. Climb steeper steps further to reach the second and third tiers, where the third tier's pool is the deepest and coolest.

A distinctive bath: you sit in a cast-iron cauldron of water heated over a wood fire, floating with herbs like lemongrass and flower petals. It's great for easing fatigue after trekking or playing in the water, and even more atmospheric with a mountain view at sunset.
A guided kayaking trip through fast-flowing stretches between rocks. Options range from a basic beginner course to routes through stronger rapids, and availability depends on the river's water level.
Float down the river on a large inner tube — easier than kayaking, making it popular with families. A guide accompanies you, and life jackets and helmets are provided.
Dip your feet in a riverside pool and let small fish nibble away dead skin. The roughly
30-minute
session often includes a short foot massage.

Rice terraces tended by the indigenous Iraynon-Bukidnon community in this mountain barangay. They're most beautiful once the green deepens after planting; visit with a local guide and be respectful of residents' daily lives.
A sandbar island about 21 nautical miles off the Tibiao coast, about
2–3 hours
by bangka. This is an expedition-style trip only possible during the calm-sea dry season, so check the boat and weather in advance.

If you can spare an extra day, add a visit to the General Fullon rice terraces, or an expedition to Seco Island during the calm-sea dry season. Both require booking transport and a guide the day before.

Lodging clusters in mountainside Barangay Tuno, close to the river and falls. Kayak Inn, a riverside lodge that has long operated alongside the kayaking trips, is known for simple cottages built of bamboo and nipa palm, while Kalawak Mountain Resort on the hillside is known for its kawa baths and treehouse-style rooms. Rates run about
a night, and small pensions and homestays are available in the coastal village. Many places have no air conditioning, so check when booking.

Being a mountain village, restaurant options are limited, and most meals are taken at your lodging. Expect a simple country table: freshwater shrimp from the river and paddy-edge vegetables simmered in coconut milk, charcoal-grilled chicken and fish, and vinegar-cured kilawin. Antique province is also known for traditionally made muscovado sugar, so brown sugar sweets or rice cakes make good snacks to bring home. Simple food can be bought at the market and small bakeries along the coastal road.
The falls trek crosses the river several times and the rocks are slippery. Closed-toe aqua shoes or trekking sandals work best.
Keep your phone and wallet in a waterproof bag. You'll get wet often during the falls and river activities.
Kayaking and tubing can be cancelled on the day depending on the river's water level. Check with your lodging in advance and book ahead.
A kawa bath is most pleasant around
as the sun goes down. In the heat of midday, getting into hot water is uncomfortable.
The village has almost no ATMs, so withdraw plenty of cash in Caticlan or Kalibo beforehand.
The mountainside has many mosquitoes and insects in the evening. Bring repellent and long clothing.
Combining this with Mararison Island in Culasi for a 2-night, 3-day tour of northern Antique lets you enjoy both the sea and the valley.

In some spots around the accommodations in mountainside Tuno, phone signals are weak or don't reach at all. Arrange your driver and time in advance for the return habal-habal ride, and save your accommodation's location and contact details offline.

Rain upstream can cause the valley water to rise within a short time. If it rains or the water turns murky, get out of the falls and river immediately, and never trek without a guide during the wet season.
The upper tiers of the falls are steep with slippery rocks. Don't climb beyond the open, designated areas.
Before jumping into any of the falls' pools, ask your guide about the water depth and rock positions.
Kawa bath water can be very hot. Keep your skin from touching the cauldron's rim, and if you have heart disease or high blood pressure, keep your soak short.
Always wear a life jacket and helmet for kayaking and tubing, and follow your guide's instructions.
The Seco Island expedition requires a long crossing of open sea, so never set out if the weather looks unstable.
Barangay Tuno, where the waterfalls and resorts are clustered, is a landslide-risk area. On
September 26, 2025

, during Severe Tropical Storm Opong, landslides and falling rocks buried the homes of seven households in Sitio Igpotoy, Tuno. If a typhoon or heavy rain is forecast, postpone mountainside stays and stay in a coastal village.
